title: Instabilities in self-consistent diagrammatic approaches and how to cure them
authors: Marcel Gievers, Herbert Eßl, Stefan Rohshap, Anna Kauch, Alessandro Toschi
abstract: While self-consistent diagrammatic approaches are widely used to compute the physical properties of correlated quantum materials, their applicability may get severely hindered precisely in the parameter regions, where the most exciting physics is observed. One of the major issues, referred to as "misleading convergence", is the tendency of iterative schemes to converge to unphysical fixed points for intermediate-to-strong electronic interactions, regardless of numerical accuracy of the computation. Here, we explicitly verify that the origin of this problem in several established self-consistent many-electron approaches, defined in the general diagrammatic framework of the boson-exchange formalism, resides exclusively in the stability condition of the respective iteration schemes, and not in an intrinsic breakdown of their self-consistent diagrammatic description. This insight enables a simple and general remedy, as recently proposed in Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 016502 (2026): The redefinition of the iterative procedure, by inverting the unstable eigendirections of the Jacobian associated to the fixed point of the self-consistent algorithm. We illustrate the successful outcome of this procedure by means of systematic calculations performed on testbed, exactly solvable, models. Our results demonstrate that the physical fixed point of the diagrammatic schemes we considered can be stabilized, de facto, across the entire parameter range, including the most challenging nonperturbative/strong-coupling regimes.
summary: This work addresses the critical issue of 'misleading convergence' in advanced diagrammatic methods used for strongly correlated materials. The authors prove that the failure is due to the iterative scheme's stability, not the underlying physics. They introduce a general remedy—inverting unstable Jacobian eigendirections—which successfully stabilizes calculations across challenging, strongly-coupled regimes.
main_problem: Self-consistent diagrammatic approaches for correlated materials suffer from 'misleading convergence,' converging to unphysical fixed points in strongly interacting regimes.
main_result: The convergence failure is shown to be an artifact of the iterative scheme's stability condition, not an intrinsic breakdown of the diagrammatic theory. A remedy involves inverting the unstable eigendirections of the Jacobian.
method: The authors analyze various self-consistent diagrammatic schemes (GW, SBE, MBE) derived from the boson-exchange formalism, focusing on the stability analysis of the iterative fixed points.
model_or_system: The study applies to general correlated quantum materials, using testbeds like the Hubbard atom (HA) and the zero-point model (ZPM) to validate the procedure.
key_observables:
Self-energies ($\Sigma_
u$), bosonic propagators ($W_r$), and the stability of the fixed point determined via the Jacobian matrix.
important_parameters: Intermediate-to-strong electronic interaction regimes, and the deviation from half-filling ($\delta\mu$).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the physical fixed point can be stabilized by modifying the iterative procedure using Jacobian inversion, distinguishing this from intrinsic LWF multivaluedness.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the self-consistency loop and the stabilization step using the Jacobian, and show the comparison of converged bosonic propagators ($	ext{Wr}$) across different schemes and parameters.
paper_structure: The paper first identifies the convergence issue, then details the BE formalism and the three classes of self-consistent schemes (TRILEX, SBE, MBE). The core contribution is demonstrating the Jacobian-based stabilization procedure, followed by testing this procedure on solvable models.
why_interesting: The mathematical techniques developed for stabilizing iterative many-body calculations (Jacobian analysis) are highly relevant for any theoretical work involving complex, non-linear self-consistent equations, such as those found in open quantum systems or non-equilibrium dynamics.
